title: Electricity and the Grid
content:
Through the 1800s, scientists turned electricity from a curiosity into usable power. Volta built the first battery (1800). Faraday showed that moving magnets generate electric current (1831) - the principle behind every generator. By the late 1800s, electricity was ready to leave the laboratory.

The practical electrical age arrived in the 1880s:
- Thomas Edison built early power stations and promoted direct current (DC) along with a practical incandescent light bulb.
- Nikola Tesla and George Westinghouse championed alternating current (AC), which can be stepped up to high voltage for efficient long-distance transmission, then stepped down for safe local use.
- AC won the 'War of the Currents' because it could move power across great distances economically.

The electrical grid - generators, transformers, and transmission lines linking power plants to homes and factories - became one of the most transformative systems ever built:
- Lighting extended productive and social hours past sundown.
- Electric motors powered factories, appliances, and tools.
- Later, electronics, computing, and communications all depended on reliable electric power.

Widespread electrification is frequently ranked as the most important engineering achievement of the modern era. Nearly every other modern technology assumes it. A society's access to dependable electricity remains one of the clearest markers of its industrial and economic development.
